title: Steak fajitas
skill: Weighing in grams and finding the yield

notes.text: Sear the steak and the vegetables in batches; a crowded pan steams instead of charring.

move.title: Weigh it raw, weigh it trimmed, weigh it cooked
move.body: Fajitas are a sear and a julienne. This week they're also a measurement: you'll weigh the steak and vegetables as bought, as trimmed, and as cooked, and work out the yield. That number is how a cook knows how much to buy.

why.title: Yield
why.body: Yield is usable weight divided by bought weight. A bell pepper loses its stem, core, and seeds, usually 15 to 20 percent. A steak loses water as it cooks, often 20 to 30 percent. Knowing both tells you how much to buy for a given plate.

why.title: A dry surface sears
why.body: A wet surface has to steam dry before it can brown. Pat the steak dry after marinating, and get the pan very hot, and the crust forms in minutes.

why.title: Rest before slicing
why.body: Fresh off the heat, the juices in a steak are under pressure. Ten minutes on the board lets them settle, so they stay in the meat instead of running onto the board.

why.title: Across the grain
why.body: Flank steak's muscle fibers run in long, visible lines. Slicing across them leaves short fibers that are tender to chew; slicing along them leaves long, tough strands.

wrong.sign: The steak is gray, not browned
wrong.fix: The pan wasn't hot enough or the steak was wet. Pat it dry and wait until the oil just starts to smoke.
Check the grain and slice across it, thinner.

wrong.sign: The peppers are soft, not charred
wrong.fix: Cook them in two batches on higher heat, and stir less.

wrong.sign: Your yield is far below the usual
wrong.fix: Check the trim: cut closer to the core next time.

quiz.q: A 400 g pepper gives 330 g of strips. What's the yield?
Why rest the steak before slicing?
choices: The juices settle and stay in the meat

quiz.q: Which way do you slice flank steak?
Why weigh in grams instead of cups?
choices: It's exact, and it's the same every time
quiz.explain: A scale doesn't care how you pack it.

substitutions.note: Warm corn tortillas in pairs so they don't crack.

steps.text: Weigh the steak, each pepper, and the onion on the scale, one at a time. Write down each weight.
Mince the garlic. In the shallow dish, mix it with the lime juice, cumin, chili powder, the steak's salt, and the steak's oil.
Turn the steak in the marinade to coat it, and leave it at room temperature.
Cut the sides off each pepper's core, lay them skin side down, trim the ribs, and cut ¼-inch strips.
Halve and peel the onion, cut off the root, and slice it ¼ inch thick from pole to pole.
steps.tip: Pole to pole, along the lines, the slices hold together in the heat.

steps.text: Weigh the trimmed peppers and onion. Divide by their raw weights to get each yield, and write it down.
Lift the steak out with the tongs and pat it dry with paper towels. Throw away the marinade.
Wash your hands and the tongs with soap.
Heat the skillet over high heat until a drop of water skitters. Add a film of the vegetables' oil and lay in the steak.
Sear without moving it, then turn it with the tongs and sear the other side.
Slide the thermometer into the side of the thickest part. It needs to read at least 145°F. If not, give it 1 more minute a side.
Move the steak to the board, tent it with foil, and let it rest.
Add the rest of the oil to the skillet over medium-high heat. Cook the peppers and onion with the vegetables' salt, stirring only now and then.
Move the vegetables to a plate. Warm the tortillas in the dry skillet, 15 seconds a side, and stack them in foil.
Find the grain of the steak and slice it ¼ inch thick across it, holding the knife at a slight angle.
Weigh the sliced steak. Divide by its raw weight for its cooking yield, and write it down.
Serve the steak and vegetables with the warm tortillas, salsa, and sour cream.
